result.abstractText:
Background/aim

The incidence of benign superior vena cava syndrome (SVCS) is increasing due to the widespread use of central venous catheters and cardiac devices. Endovascular therapy is a first-line treatment option; however, recanalization of a completely occluded SVC remains technically challenging, and long-term stent patency data are limited. We report a case of central venous catheter-related benign SVCS treated with stent placement using a sharp recanalization technique and present the resulting 10-year patency outcome.

Case report

A male patient in his 50s presented with facial and upper extremity edema secondary to benign SVCS caused by repeated central venous catheter placement for short-bowel syndrome. Venography revealed complete SVC occlusion (modified Stanford type 4). Sharp recanalization using a trans-septal needle was performed under biplane fluoroscopy and cone-beam computed tomography guidance, followed by placement of a self-expanding bare-metal stent (14 × 40 mm). Symptoms resolved the following day. In-stent re-stenosis occurred at 10 months and was successfully managed with balloon dilatation, after which the stent remained patent with no recurrence of SVCS on annual follow-up. Long-term patency of the stent was achieved for the next 10 years.

Conclusion

Sharp recanalization using a trans-septal needle enabled safe and effective stent placement for completely occluded benign SVC. Long-term stent patency of 10 years was achieved with a single re-intervention, demonstrating that this technique is a viable treatment option for benign SVCS.

result.abstractText:
Objectives

Plastic stents (PS) are widely used for biliary drainage, with occlusion mainly caused by biofilm formation and sludge accumulation. However, direct evaluation of luminal occlusion remains limited, and its spatial distribution is poorly understood. This study aimed to quantify luminal occlusion in retrieved PS and identify associated factors.

Methods

In this prospective observational study, 64 patients (196 stents) undergoing scheduled PS exchange at approximately 3-month intervals were included. Retrieved stents were divided into proximal, central, and distal segments, and occlusion was quantified using ImageJ. Clinical, microbiological, and device-related variables were analyzed. Multivariable linear regression was used to identify independent factors associated with occlusion.

Results

The mean occlusion rate was 28.8% ± 29.8%. Occlusion was significantly higher in the proximal segment than in the central and distal segments (35.5% vs. 25.8% and 25.0%; p < 0.05). Multivariable analysis showed that age > 65 years (β = 11.62, p = 0.006), Enterococcus-positive bile culture (β = 16.00, p = 0.012), and probiotic use (β = 14.91, p = 0.007) were independently associated with increased occlusion. Stent brand was also associated with the degree of occlusion.

Conclusions

Plastic stent occlusion is segment-dependent, predominantly affecting the proximal portion, and is associated with microbiological and material-related factors. Direct quantification may help optimize stent design and management.
